An elbow-length-sleeved straight-cut cotton T-shirt, a real plain T-shirt and not a real garment, covered edge to edge in a clean vector illustration print with flat colour fills, designed to make the shirt look like the outfit of a teacher in a feminine-styled version. The print is cut to the T-shirt's shape, so the shirt itself looks like the outfit being worn, with the sleeves as the outfit's sleeves. The outfit is printed across the whole front, over the shoulders and down both sleeves, showing a tweed jacket with chalk-dusted elbow patches. Turn the shirt around and the back carries the matching back of the outfit, printed edge to edge with nothing left plain. One continuous print of the outfit's cloth covers the shirt from collar band to hem and out to both sleeve hems. It is an ordinary T-shirt in shape, with a straight open hem and sleeves cut to match the outfit's sleeves. The shirt is an ordinary T-shirt ending in a straight bottom hem, and the garment printed on it runs straight down the whole shirt to that hem. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The outfit is laid out on the shirt's own rectangle shape, fully covering it from side seam to side seam. The shirt's sleeves are tailored to end at the elbow, exactly where the outfit's sleeves end. Everything is flat ink on opaque cotton, lace, tulle, fur, feathers, sequins, armour and metal appear as printed patterns. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. It also shows printed cuffs and wrists at the sleeve hems. The illusion is purely flat and two-dimensional, with no real fabric, buttons or pockets beyond the print. The tee is clearly a costume tee, not a plain shirt, it shows the footwear's trim colours as stripes on the cuffs and hem, the outfit's patches, insignia and emblems and the belt, straps and buckles of the outfit, so anyone can tell at a glance what outfit it stands for. Any printed skin, such as hands, wrists, neck, chest or forearms, is in a flat printed very deep brown skin tone.

The shirt's neckline is the outfit's collar opening, the shirt's sleeves carry the outfit's sleeves, and the shirt's hem is the outfit's lower edge, showing a thick Aran sweater with an oilskin smock. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. The outfit's own cloth covers the whole shirt as one continuous print, so shoulders, sleeves and body are all in the outfit's colours. The shirt keeps the outline of an ordinary T-shirt, round neckline, straight side seams, sleeves, and a straight open hem. The shirt is an ordinary T-shirt ending in a straight bottom hem, and the garment printed on it runs straight down the whole shirt to that hem. The print is cut exactly to the shirt, neck, shoulders, armholes, sleeves and hem are all covered in the outfit's own fabric. The outfit is stretched to the shirt's own straight-sided shape and fills it completely, so it suits any body size. The shirt is a long-sleeved T-shirt matching the outfit's long sleeves, printed with the sleeves and cuffs all the way down to the wrist hems. The shirt is solid opaque cotton and every texture and sheen is a printed picture. Only the outfit's fabric, trims and fastenings are pictured, spread across the entire shirt as a continuous pattern. The printed collar and lapels line up with the shirt's actual neckline. It carries enough of the costume to be unmistakable, the outfit's patches, insignia and emblems, its pockets, flaps and trims and the headwear's emblem or crest worked into the chest, all in the outfit's own colours. Any printed skin, such as hands, wrists, neck, chest or forearms, is in a flat printed very deep brown skin tone.

The outfit's front panels run straight down the shirt's front with its shoulders sitting on the shirt's shoulder seams, and its sleeves are printed along the shirt's sleeves to cuffs at the sleeve hems, showing a pinstripe suit with braces and a loud tie. Front and back are both fully printed, the back showing how the same outfit looks from behind. One continuous print of the outfit's cloth covers the shirt from collar band to hem and out to both sleeve hems. The shirt keeps the outline of an ordinary T-shirt, round neckline, straight side seams, sleeves, and a straight open hem. Only the upper garment is printed, running all the way down to the shirt's straight hem. The outfit's collar meets the real collar band, its shoulders sit on the real shoulder seams and its sleeves fill the real sleeves, all in one piece of printed cloth. The uniform fills the whole straight-sided shirt shape edge to edge, the same width at chest, waist and hem. A long-sleeved shirt is used so the outfit's long sleeves fit exactly, printed full length to the shirt's wrist hems. Everything is flat ink on opaque cotton, lace, tulle, fur, feathers, sequins, armour and metal appear as printed patterns. The picture is only the garment, its cloth, seams, buttons and trims laid flat across the whole shirt like a sewing pattern. It also shows printed gloves emerging at the sleeve hems. The illusion is purely flat and two-dimensional, with no real fabric, buttons or pockets beyond the print. The tee is clearly a costume tee, not a plain shirt, it shows the lower garment's colours and pattern as a band across the hem, the most recognisable props and accessories of the outfit as appliqué pieces and its pockets, flaps and trims, so anyone can tell at a glance what outfit it stands for. Any printed skin, such as hands, wrists, neck, chest or forearms, is in a flat printed very deep brown skin tone.
